title: Processes & Threads
description: Learn the difference between programs, processes, threads, process states, and context switching.
intro: A program is stored instructions; a process is a running instance with execution state and resources. A process commonly has an address space and operating-system-managed attributes, while threads within a process share many resources but maintain their own execution state and stack. The OS schedules runnable threads or processes and switches execution when needed.
learningObjectives: Explain Process in your own words.
Explain Thread in your own words.
Explain Ready state in your own words.
Apply Blocked or waiting state or a related concept to a practical situation.

sections.title: Process
sections.explanation:
A process is an executing program instance with operating-system-managed state and resources such as an address space and open handles.

Why it matters: The OS generally manages them as distinct process instances even if they execute the same program file.

Common misunderstanding: A program file on disk and a running process are exactly the same object.
sections.howItWorks: Track the process identifier, execution state, resources, and transitions. A process is more than a running program file, and threads within one process share selected resources. Apply that approach to this example: Two separate instances of a text editor run at the same time. Expected interpretation: The OS generally manages them as distinct process instances even if they execute the same program file.
sections.example: Two separate instances of a text editor run at the same time.
sections.outcome: The OS generally manages them as distinct process instances even if they execute the same program file.
sections.commonMisconception: A program file on disk and a running process are exactly the same object.
sections.takeaway: Remember: Process — A process is an executing program instance with operating-system-managed state and resources such as an address space and open handles.

sections.title: Thread
sections.explanation:
A thread is an execution path within a process; threads of the same process commonly share its address space and process resources.

Why it matters: Threads can share process memory, while each thread maintains execution-specific state such as registers and a stack.

Common misunderstanding: Every thread has a completely separate copy of all process memory by definition.
sections.howItWorks: Track the process identifier, execution state, resources, and transitions. A process is more than a running program file, and threads within one process share selected resources. Apply that approach to this example: A browser uses multiple threads to handle work concurrently within one process. Expected interpretation: Threads can share process memory, while each thread maintains execution-specific state such as registers and a stack.
sections.example: A browser uses multiple threads to handle work concurrently within one process.
sections.outcome: Threads can share process memory, while each thread maintains execution-specific state such as registers and a stack.
sections.commonMisconception: Every thread has a completely separate copy of all process memory by definition.
sections.takeaway: Remember: Thread — A thread is an execution path within a process; threads of the same process commonly share its address space and process resources.

sections.title: Ready state
sections.explanation:
A ready process or thread is able to run but is waiting for CPU scheduling rather than waiting for an event or resource.

Why it matters: Some remain ready until the scheduler selects them for CPU execution.

Common misunderstanding: A ready thread is necessarily blocked waiting for disk input.
sections.howItWorks: Track the process identifier, execution state, resources, and transitions. A process is more than a running program file, and threads within one process share selected resources. Apply that approach to this example: Several compute-bound threads are runnable on a one-core system. Expected interpretation: Some remain ready until the scheduler selects them for CPU execution.
sections.example: Several compute-bound threads are runnable on a one-core system.
sections.outcome: Some remain ready until the scheduler selects them for CPU execution.
sections.commonMisconception: A ready thread is necessarily blocked waiting for disk input.
sections.takeaway: Remember: Ready state — A ready process or thread is able to run but is waiting for CPU scheduling rather than waiting for an event or resource.

sections.title: Blocked or waiting state
sections.explanation:
A blocked task cannot continue until a specified event or resource becomes available, such as I/O completion or a lock.

Why it matters: The task waits for the event rather than continuously consuming a CPU time slice in a normal blocking operation.

Common misunderstanding: A blocked process is always using the CPU at 100 percent while it waits.
sections.howItWorks: Track the process identifier, execution state, resources, and transitions. A process is more than a running program file, and threads within one process share selected resources. Apply that approach to this example: A process is waiting for a file read to complete. Expected interpretation: The task waits for the event rather than continuously consuming a CPU time slice in a normal blocking operation.
sections.example: A process is waiting for a file read to complete.
sections.outcome: The task waits for the event rather than continuously consuming a CPU time slice in a normal blocking operation.
sections.commonMisconception: A blocked process is always using the CPU at 100 percent while it waits.
sections.takeaway: Remember: Blocked or waiting state — A blocked task cannot continue until a specified event or resource becomes available, such as I/O completion or a lock.

sections.title: Context switch
sections.explanation:
A context switch saves enough execution state for one task and restores state for another, allowing the CPU to resume different work.

Why it matters: The OS performs a context switch when required, which has overhead and does not itself perform useful application work.

Common misunderstanding: A context switch means the computer copied the whole process memory to disk.
sections.howItWorks: Track the process identifier, execution state, resources, and transitions. A process is more than a running program file, and threads within one process share selected resources. Apply that approach to this example: A timer interrupt lets the scheduler run another ready task. Expected interpretation: The OS performs a context switch when required, which has overhead and does not itself perform useful application work.
sections.example: A timer interrupt lets the scheduler run another ready task.
sections.outcome: The OS performs a context switch when required, which has overhead and does not itself perform useful application work.
sections.commonMisconception: A context switch means the computer copied the whole process memory to disk.
sections.takeaway: Remember: Context switch — A context switch saves enough execution state for one task and restores state for another, allowing the CPU to resume different work.

sections.title: Round-robin
sections.explanation:
Round-robin schedules runnable tasks in turn, allowing each to run for a bounded time quantum before moving on if it remains runnable.

Why it matters: Each task receives a turn, supporting interactive responsiveness and preventing one task from monopolizing the CPU under the model assumptions.

sections.title: Time quantum
sections.explanation:

sections.title: Waiting time
sections.explanation:
Waiting time measures the time a task spends waiting in the ready queue under a defined scheduling model, distinct from its CPU burst time.

title: Concurrency, Synchronization & Deadlocks
description: Understand race conditions, critical sections, locks, semaphores, and the conditions that can produce deadlock.
intro: Concurrency means tasks can make progress during overlapping periods, even on a single CPU through interleaving. Shared mutable state creates risks when operations are not atomic. Synchronization tools coordinate access, while deadlock occurs when tasks wait in a cycle that prevents progress. Correct concurrency design requires reasoning about invariants, ordering, blocking, and failure paths.

sections.title: Race condition
sections.explanation:
A race condition occurs when a result depends on the timing or interleaving of operations that are not adequately coordinated.

Why it matters: One increment may be lost unless the read-modify-write operation is protected or made atomic.

Common misunderstanding: A race condition only occurs when two programs run on two physical CPU cores.
sections.howItWorks: Identify shared state and the exact operation that must be atomic. Then determine what synchronization protects the critical section and whether the lock order can create a deadlock. Apply that approach to this example: Two threads read the same counter value, increment locally, and write the same next value. Expected interpretation: One increment may be lost unless the read-modify-write operation is protected or made atomic.
sections.example: Two threads read the same counter value, increment locally, and write the same next value.
sections.outcome: One increment may be lost unless the read-modify-write operation is protected or made atomic.
sections.commonMisconception: A race condition only occurs when two programs run on two physical CPU cores.
sections.takeaway: Remember: Race condition — A race condition occurs when a result depends on the timing or interleaving of operations that are not adequately coordinated.

sections.title: Critical section
sections.explanation:
A critical section is code that accesses shared state and must obey a synchronization invariant to avoid conflicting operations.

Why it matters: Use an appropriate synchronization strategy to prevent unsafe concurrent entry or conflicting mutation.

Common misunderstanding: A critical section is any part of code that runs slowly and therefore must be moved to a separate thread.
sections.howItWorks: Identify shared state and the exact operation that must be atomic. Then determine what synchronization protects the critical section and whether the lock order can create a deadlock. Apply that approach to this example: Two threads update a shared data structure that cannot safely be modified concurrently. Expected interpretation: Use an appropriate synchronization strategy to prevent unsafe concurrent entry or conflicting mutation.
sections.example: Two threads update a shared data structure that cannot safely be modified concurrently.
sections.outcome: Use an appropriate synchronization strategy to prevent unsafe concurrent entry or conflicting mutation.
sections.commonMisconception: A critical section is any part of code that runs slowly and therefore must be moved to a separate thread.
sections.takeaway: Remember: Critical section — A critical section is code that accesses shared state and must obey a synchronization invariant to avoid conflicting operations.

sections.title: Mutex
sections.explanation:
A mutex provides mutual exclusion around a protected region, normally allowing one owner at a time according to the API's rules.

Why it matters: Guard the update with a mutex and ensure every path releases it correctly, including error paths.

Common misunderstanding: A mutex automatically makes every operation in the entire program thread-safe.
sections.howItWorks: Identify shared state and the exact operation that must be atomic. Then determine what synchronization protects the critical section and whether the lock order can create a deadlock. Apply that approach to this example: Several threads must update one shared counter safely. Expected interpretation: Guard the update with a mutex and ensure every path releases it correctly, including error paths.
sections.example: Several threads must update one shared counter safely.
sections.outcome: Guard the update with a mutex and ensure every path releases it correctly, including error paths.
sections.commonMisconception: A mutex automatically makes every operation in the entire program thread-safe.
sections.takeaway: Remember: Mutex — A mutex provides mutual exclusion around a protected region, normally allowing one owner at a time according to the API's rules.

sections.title: Semaphore
sections.explanation:
A semaphore maintains a counter used to coordinate access or signaling; a counting semaphore can represent a limited number of available resources.

Why it matters: A counting semaphore initialized to five can limit concurrent users, provided acquisition and release are balanced.

Common misunderstanding: A semaphore and a mutex are identical concepts with identical ownership semantics in every API.
sections.howItWorks: Identify shared state and the exact operation that must be atomic. Then determine what synchronization protects the critical section and whether the lock order can create a deadlock. Apply that approach to this example: A service may allow only five tasks to use a constrained resource concurrently. Expected interpretation: A counting semaphore initialized to five can limit concurrent users, provided acquisition and release are balanced.
sections.example: A service may allow only five tasks to use a constrained resource concurrently.
sections.outcome: A counting semaphore initialized to five can limit concurrent users, provided acquisition and release are balanced.
sections.commonMisconception: A semaphore and a mutex are identical concepts with identical ownership semantics in every API.
sections.takeaway: Remember: Semaphore — A semaphore maintains a counter used to coordinate access or signaling; a counting semaphore can represent a limited number of available resources.

sections.title: Deadlock
sections.explanation:
Deadlock is a state where tasks wait indefinitely for resources or events held by one another, with no task able to make progress in the cycle.

Why it matters: The circular wait can deadlock both threads unless the design breaks a necessary condition or uses another recovery strategy.

Common misunderstanding: Any waiting or slow program is necessarily deadlocked.
sections.howItWorks: Identify shared state and the exact operation that must be atomic. Then determine what synchronization protects the critical section and whether the lock order can create a deadlock. Apply that approach to this example: Thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2 while thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1. Expected interpretation: The circular wait can deadlock both threads unless the design breaks a necessary condition or uses another recovery strategy.
sections.example: Thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2 while thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1.
sections.outcome: The circular wait can deadlock both threads unless the design breaks a necessary condition or uses another recovery strategy.
sections.commonMisconception: Any waiting or slow program is necessarily deadlocked.
sections.takeaway: Remember: Deadlock — Deadlock is a state where tasks wait indefinitely for resources or events held by one another, with no task able to make progress in the cycle.

title: Memory Management & Virtual Memory
description: Understand address spaces, paging, page tables, TLBs, page faults, and memory pressure.
intro: Virtual memory gives a process an address space that the OS and hardware translate into physical memory. Paging divides virtual and physical memory into fixed-size units, while page tables track mappings and the translation lookaside buffer (TLB) caches recent translations. A page fault indicates that access requires OS handling; depending on the cause, it may be resolved normally or be an invalid access.

sections.title: Virtual address space
sections.explanation:
A virtual address space is the set of addresses a process can use, mapped and protected by OS/hardware mechanisms rather than directly representing all physical RAM.

Why it matters: Their address spaces can map that virtual address to different physical locations while maintaining process isolation.

Common misunderstanding: Every virtual address is a permanent direct physical address and is shared identically by all processes.

sections.takeaway: Remember: Virtual address space — A virtual address space is the set of addresses a process can use, mapped and protected by OS/hardware mechanisms rather than directly representing all physical RAM.

sections.title: Page table
sections.explanation:
A page table records virtual-to-physical page mappings and associated permission/status information used during address translation.

Why it matters: The memory-management hardware and OS use page-table information to determine the physical page and access permissions.

Common misunderstanding: A page table is a directory listing of files stored on a disk.

sections.outcome: The memory-management hardware and OS use page-table information to determine the physical page and access permissions.

sections.takeaway: Remember: Page table — A page table records virtual-to-physical page mappings and associated permission/status information used during address translation.

sections.title: TLB
sections.explanation:
A translation lookaside buffer caches recent address translations to speed up virtual-to-physical address translation.

Why it matters: TLB hits can avoid a full page-table walk for those translations.

Common misunderstanding: The TLB is the same thing as the CPU's application data cache and stores the actual contents of all RAM pages.

Virtual addresses are not direct promises of a fixed physical location. Apply that approach to this example: A program repeatedly accesses memory pages whose translations remain in the TLB. Expected interpretation: TLB hits can avoid a full page-table walk for those translations.

sections.title: Page fault
sections.explanation:
A page fault occurs when memory access requires page-related OS handling, such as loading a nonresident valid page or rejecting an invalid/prohibited access.

Why it matters: The OS may fetch the page into memory, update mappings, and resume the process; an invalid access may instead raise an error.

Common misunderstanding: Every page fault means the application crashed because its pointer was invalid.

Expected interpretation: The OS may fetch the page into memory, update mappings, and resume the process; an invalid access may instead raise an error.

sections.outcome: The OS may fetch the page into memory, update mappings, and resume the process; an invalid access may instead raise an error.

sections.takeaway: Remember: Page fault — A page fault occurs when memory access requires page-related OS handling, such as loading a nonresident valid page or rejecting an invalid/prohibited access.

sections.title: Thrashing
sections.explanation:
Thrashing occurs when a system spends excessive time moving pages rather than doing useful work, commonly under severe memory pressure.

Why it matters: Reduce memory pressure or working-set demand and investigate the competing workload rather than expecting more paging to fix it.

Common misunderstanding: Thrashing means the CPU is performing more useful application computation than usual.

sections.title: File metadata
sections.explanation:
File metadata stores properties such as ownership, permissions, size, and timestamps in addition to the file's content bytes.

Why it matters: The metadata can cause one user to access a file while another is denied, despite matching content.

Why it matters: The OS resolves the path through directory entries and checks required access along the path and on the file.

sections.title: Interrupt
sections.explanation:
An interrupt signals the processor that an event needs attention, allowing the system to run an appropriate handler according to architecture and OS rules.

Why it matters: The OS can handle the completion and make the waiting task eligible to continue.

sections.title: Polling
sections.explanation:
Polling repeatedly checks a device or condition to discover whether an event has occurred.

Why it matters: Polling may be useful in some designs but can waste CPU work if performed too aggressively for a long wait.

Direct Memory Access allows a capable device/controller to transfer data to or from memory with limited per-byte CPU involvement, coordinated by the system.

description: Follow the path from firmware through bootloader and kernel to userspace and understand Linux distributions.
intro: A boot sequence initializes hardware and transfers control through several stages before user applications are available. Modern systems commonly begin with firmware, select a boot entry, load a bootloader and kernel, initialize early userspace, and start the system's main service manager or equivalent. Linux is technically the kernel; a Linux distribution packages it with user-space tools, libraries, an installer, package management, and policies.

sections.title: Firmware

Platform firmware initializes hardware and selects or launches a boot path before the main operating system starts.

sections.title: Bootloader
sections.explanation:
A bootloader loads or helps select the operating-system kernel and required boot configuration, then transfers control according to its design.

intro: A Linux service may run in the background and be supervised by an init or service manager. intro: Storage troubleshooting separates device discovery, partitions, filesystems, mount state, free data blocks, and inode availability. sections.explanation:
A block device exposes storage in addressable blocks and may represent a disk, virtual volume, or partition.

title: Virtualization & Containers
description: Distinguish virtual machines, hypervisors, containers, images, isolation, and resource boundaries.
intro: Virtual machines virtualize hardware and run separate guest operating systems under a hypervisor. Containers typically share the host kernel while isolating process, filesystem, network, and resource views through OS mechanisms. Both approaches can improve reproducibility and isolation, but they have different security boundaries, startup costs, compatibility constraints, and operational requirements. A container is not simply a lightweight VM in every technical sense.

sections.title: Virtual machine
sections.explanation:
A virtual machine presents virtual hardware to a guest operating system managed by a hypervisor or platform virtualization layer.

Why it matters: The guest OS manages its own processes and kernel while the hypervisor allocates host resources.

Common misunderstanding: A VM must always share the host kernel and cannot run a different OS kernel.

Expected interpretation: The guest OS manages its own processes and kernel while the hypervisor allocates host resources.

sections.outcome: The guest OS manages its own processes and kernel while the hypervisor allocates host resources.

sections.takeaway: Remember: Virtual machine — A virtual machine presents virtual hardware to a guest operating system managed by a hypervisor or platform virtualization layer.

sections.title: Hypervisor
sections.explanation:

sections.title: Security updates
sections.explanation:
Security updates remediate known vulnerabilities and should be planned, applied, and verified according to system and service requirements.

Why it matters: Review the update and impact, follow the approved change process, apply the fix, and verify service health afterward.

Common misunderstanding: If a server is behind a firewall, patching its known vulnerabilities is unnecessary.
sections.howItWorks: Apply least privilege, minimize exposed services, update deliberately, protect credentials and logs, and verify that a recovery path works. No single hardening setting guarantees security. Apply that approach to this example: A production Linux server runs an outdated package with a relevant security fix available. Expected interpretation: Review the update and impact, follow the approved change process, apply the fix, and verify service health afterward.

sections.title: SSH key authentication
sections.explanation:
SSH public-key authentication uses a public/private key relationship to prove client identity according to server policy; private keys must remain protected.

Why it matters: Use an approved key, protect its private portion, and configure account and server policy intentionally.

Common misunderstanding: The public key must be kept secret while the private key can be shared with other users.

sections.title: Service exposure
sections.explanation:
Reducing service exposure means limiting listeners, network paths, and firewall policy to the interfaces and clients that require access.

Why it matters: Consider binding it to loopback or a restricted interface and enforce suitable access policy, then verify functionality.

Common misunderstanding: Moving a service to a less common port alone makes it secure against unauthorized access.

sections.title: Backup and recovery
sections.explanation:
Backups preserve recoverable data or system state and should be tested through restoration, with access and retention protected from the same failures as production.

Why it matters: Perform a controlled restoration test and verify integrity, completeness, and recovery objectives.

Common misunderstanding: A successful backup command guarantees data can be restored within the required time.

workedExample.title: Harden a small Linux service host
workedExample.context: A Linux VM hosts a test web application and remote administration is needed only from a trusted lab network.
steps: Inventory listening services and disable only unused services after checking dependencies.
Update packages according to a safe change plan and confirm the application remains healthy.
Restrict management access to the approved network and use protected SSH authentication.
Run services with least privilege, review logs, and test restoration of important lab data.
workedExample.result: Hardening combines reduced exposure, identity controls, patching, monitoring, and recovery—not one magic setting.
